body.text: Geography also limits the NSR’s usefulness. Although the route can accommodate some large vessels, ice conditions, navigational restrictions and limited infrastructure constrain its capacity to handle the enormous volumes carried through conventional shipping corridors. Furthermore, the NSR primarily benefits trade between Europe and Northeast Asia. It offers little advantage for shipments originating in the Persian Gulf or travelling between Asia and destinations outside northern Europe.

For most shipping companies, diverting vessels around the Cape of Good Hope remains a more practical response to disruptions in the Red Sea. However, this diversion cannot circumvent the Strait of Hormuz for cargo originating inside the Persian Gulf. Although this adds distance and fuel costs, the route accommodates the world’s largest commercial vessels and operates year-round without Arctic ice restrictions.

Nevertheless, the Arctic could provide some relief through energy production rather than container shipping. Russian Arctic hydrocarbons could reach Asian consumers without passing through Hormuz or Bab el-Mandeb.

Russia’s Vostok Oil project began exports in September 2026, while the sanctioned Arctic LNG 2 project has demonstrated its ability to produce LNG despite logistical difficulties. Both projects could eventually contribute additional hydrocarbons to international markets, reducing dependence on supplies passing through Middle Eastern chokepoints. However, production and shipping constraints limit these projects’ immediate contribution, while redirecting existing exports would do little to increase global output.

Expanding these projects would also present Western governments with an uncomfortable choice: whether improving energy security justifies relaxing sanctions that constrain Russia’s ability to finance its war against Ukraine.

China is particularly well positioned to benefit from growing Russian Arctic energy exports, having invested in Arctic energy projects and participated in NSR shipping. Japan also has investments in Russian LNG developments, while South Korea and India have explored Arctic maritime opportunities. However, sanctions and political considerations complicate their participation, particularly for US allies Japan and South Korea.

The Middle East crisis is unlikely to turn the Arctic into an alternative Suez Canal. Instead, it may reinforce a different development: the importance of Russian Arctic energy to Asian markets, even as Western sanctions limit the region’s potential.
